full_judgment:
Md Muzzammel Hossain CJ: I have gone through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my brothers, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J. and Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the reasoning and findings given by, Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J.

Surendra Kumar Sinha J: I have had the advantage of reading the draft copy of the judgment prepared by my learned brother Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. While agreeing with the conclusion arrived at by my learned brother that the appeal and the connected petition be dismissed, as some vital questions of law are involved in these matters, it is desirable that I should add something of my own.

<u>3. The pivotal question which arises for consideration in these matters is whether the Administrator of Waqfs can accord sanction for transferring any part of the Waqf property by way of lease exceeding 5(five) years in exercise of its power under section 56 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 or in the alternative, a mutawalli of a waqf estate can transfer by lease in perpetuity any part of the waqf property with prior approval of the Administrator. An opinion on the point requires consideration of the facts which are succinctly narrated below:</u>

Appellant is a mutawalli of a Waqf Estate who instituted Title Suit No. 26 of 1992 (the plaintiff) against the respondent Nos.1-3 seeking nullity of lease deed dated 18th May, 1965 executed by his father Ahidulla as mutawalli of the waqf eatate in favour of respondent Nos. 1 (the defendant) on the ground that his father though executed the lease deed in respect of the suit land measuring an area of 0.92 acre, he did not pay the salami and rent and also did not take over possession of the suit land and thus, the defendant violated the terms of the lease deed, and that the lease was not acted upon. Defendant also instituted Title Suit No. 38 of 1992 seeking declaration of title in respect of 1st schedule land and for recovery of khas possession in respect of 2nd schedule land measuring an area of 0.04 (0.03) acre. His case is that the plaintiff's father Ashidulla, the mutawalli, with prior sanction of the Administrator of Waqfs leased out 0.92 acre of land of plot No.932 at a premium of Taka 300 and handed over possession on the same day. He developed the land and constructed houses in a portion of the land. He also purchased 0.04 acre of land of plot No. 933 situated contiguous to the suit plot for path way and mutated his name, paid rent and taxes to the authorities and thereafter, he was dispossessed from the 2nd schedule of land taking advantage of his temporary absence from the suit land. Appellant's defence case in the latter suit is similar to that of his plaint case and vice versa.

4. The trial Court heard both the suits analogously and held that the plaintiff-appellant had no title and possession in the suit land; that the suit without seeking consequential relief is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act; that the defendant acquired title in pursuance of lease deed dated 18th May, 1965; that he is in possession of a portion of the suit land but, he failed to prove the portion in which he is in specific possession and that the defendant's claim of dispossession in respect of the second schedule land by the plaintiff by raising 4(four) thatched huts is inconsistent with his pleadings. With these findings the trial Court dismissed both the suits. Two appeals were filed, one by the plaintiff and the other by the defendant being Title Appeal Nos. 57 of 1995 and 182 of 1995 respectively. The Court of Appeal below allowed Title Appeal No. 57 of 1995, decreed Title Suit No.26 of 1992 and declared the impugned deed void and not binding upon the plaintiff, dismissed Title Appeal No.182 of 1990 and thereby affirmed the judgment of the trial Court dismissing Title Suit No. 38 of 1992. Feeling aggrieved by the said judgments, the defendant moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos. 2571 and 2572 of 1998. A Single Bench of the High Court Division heard both the rules analogously and by the impugned judgment made both the rules absolute, set aside the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit Nos. 26 of 1992 and sent back the Title Suit No. 38 of 1992 to the trial Court for writing out a fresh judgment for deciding the defendant's claim of possession and dispossession in respect of e schedule land on the basis of the evidence available with the record. The learned Judge noticed that there are conflicting findings as regards the finding of possession followed by dispossession as claimed by the defendant in respect of the 2nd schedule land.

5. After remand, the trial Court dismissed the suit, but the Court of Appeal below believed the defendant's case of possession followed by dispossession and decreed the suit declaring the defendant's title in the suit land and allowing the prayer for recovery of khas possession in respect of 0.03 acre of land. Plaintiff moved a revision petition in the High Court Division which affirmed the judgment of the Court of Appeal below observing that the Court of Appeal below rightly found on the basis of the evidence that the plaintiff dispossessed the defendant in respect of 0.03 acre of land and that the plaintiff could not point out any misreading or non-consideration of the evidence on record. The High Court Division rightly found that the defendant has been able to prove his title in the suit land and that the plaintiff has dispossessed the defendant in respect of 0.03 acre of land without due process of law and thereby, it has committed no illegality in maintaining the judgment of the Court of Appeal below. More so, the leave petition is also barred by 242 days and the explanation offered for the delay is not satisfactory. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan appearing for the plain-tiff also finds it difficult to assail the judgment of the High Court Division.

6. It was urged on behalf of the appellant that the High Court Division misconstrued section 56 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 and illegally held that a mutawalli of a waqf estate can transfer a portion of the waqf property by lease exceeding five years in failing to notice that such lease tantamount to absolute transfer which is not intended by the legislature. It was further urged that the Administrator has power to accord sanction of grant of lease for a limited period, inasmuch as, the use of coma (,) after the word 'exchange' in sub-section (1) of section 56, and the use of words 'or by way of lease for a term exceeding 5 years' thereafter manifestly suggest that a mutawalli has no power even, with prior sanction of the Administrator to grant lease of any part of the waqf property in perpetuity.

7. Points raised require analytical consideration of certain provisions of the Waqfs Ordinance and other laws relevant for the disposal of the in matters. Sections 27 to 46 have been placed in Chapter III of the Ordinance under the heading "Powers and Functions of the Administrator and the Committee" like saplings in a row. Section 27 relates to the general powers and functions of the Administrator which include investigation and determination of the nature and extent of waqfs and waqf properties, inspection of accounts, returns for ensuring that the waqf properties and income arising there from are applied to the objects and for the benefit of any class of persons for which such waqfs are created and to give direction for proper administration of the Waqfs, etc. Section 28 deals with general powers and functions of the Committee, which consists as per section 20, the Administrator as chairman and ten members to be appointed by the Government, of whom, one shall be a mutawalli of the Shia Sect, three from the mutawallis of Sunnis sect and the remaining six shall be from among the prominent, respectable and benevolent citizens of Muslim community. Section 32 authorizes the Administrator of Waqfs to remove the mutawalli in cases covered by clauses I-IV of sub-section (1). Sub-section (4) of section 32 authorizes the Administrator to appoint a new mutawalli under the circumstances mentioned therein. Section 33 empowers the Administrator of Waqfs to transfer any part of a waqf i property with previous sanction of the Government for the improvement and benefit of the waqf, and section 34 empowers to take administration, control, management and maintenance of any waqf property.

8. According to Mr Bhuiyan, the power of sanction for transfer of a portion of the waqf Property has exclusively been given to the Government and section 33 shall override the other provisions of the Ordinance, in view of the non-obstante clause "notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in this Ordinance", used in it. This section, it is contended, shall prevail despite anything contrary contained in any other provision, i.e. section 56 of the Ordinance, which authorizes a mutawalli of any immovable property of a waqf to transfer by sale, gift, mortgage or exchange, or by way of lease for a term exceeding 5 years with previous sanction of the Administrator. True, this clause is used in contradiction to the expression 'subject to' any other provision of the Ordinance, but when the non-obstante clause refers to the provision of a statute in general, the intention of the legislature must be determined and the clause has to be construed accordingly. It is often used by way of abundant caution, but mainly used as a legislative device, in case of conflict to give the provision containing non-obstante clause an overriding effect over any other provision of the statute. But, when the two provisions are apparently inconsistent, it is the duty of the Court to harmoniously interpret those provisions so that both the provisions may be operative. Reference in this connection is the case of Dominion of India vs Shribai A. Arabinda Bose, AIR 1955 SC 296 in which, it has been observed:

"Although ordinarily there should be a close approximation between the non-obstante clause and the operative part of the section, the non-obstante clause need not necessarily and always be coextensive with the operative part, so as to have the effect of cutting down the clear terms of an enactment. If the words of the enactment are clear and are capable of only one interpretation on a plain and grammatical construction of the words thereof a non-obstante clause cannot cut down the construction and restrict the scope of its operation. In such cases the non-obstante clause has to be read as clarifying the whole position and must be understood to have been incorporated in the enactment by the legislature by way of abundant caution and not by way of limiting the ambit and scope of the operative part of the enactment."

<u>9. What's more, I find no inconsistency between the two provisions. Section 33 deals with the power of the Administrator to transfer waqf property when he is in charge of such property in the absence of the mutawalli. This section is found in chapter III, whereas, section 56 is found in Chapter VI under the heading 'Transfer of Waqfs Property.' These two chapters provide for two distinct purposes. It is established principle that the duty of the Court is to effectuate the purpose of an enactment and not to defeat it. In Bates, (1965)1 WLR 1133 (1147), Lord Denning, MR stated the object is to ascertain the intention of the legislature. This intention must be discovered, of course, from the words which they have used but the words must be sensibly interpreted. We are not here to make nonsense of them. If we look at the history, the practice of grouping sections of an Act under different headings was first introduced in UK in 1845 in the Clauses Consolidation Acts (Thring, Practical legislation, Ed.1902). According to Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes, 12th Edn. page 11, the headings pre-fixed to sections or sets of sections in some modern statutes are regarded as preambles of those sections. They cannot control the plain words of the statute but they may explain ambiguous words'. Head notes may, in some cases, be looked upon in the light of preambles if there is any ambiguity in the meaning of the sections on which they throw light. The arrangement of sections into parts and their headings are substantive parts of the Act and as is pointed out by Craies on Statute Law, 5th Edn, page 165, 'they are gradually winning recognition as a kind of preamble to the enactments which they precede limiting or explaining their operations'. The above views make no hesitation in arriving at the conclusion that sections 33 and 56 deal with different subjects showing operation in separate fields and are not intended to overlap so as to restrict each other.</u>

10. We have the privilege of hearing Mr Mahmudul Islam as amicus curiae. Learned amicus curiae argued that sections 33 and 56 do not conflict with each other for, the sections are found in two chapters for different objects. Section 56 does not restrict permanent lease by a mutawalli provided that the mutawalli has obtained previous sanction of the Administrator. In this connection he has referred to the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 56 which, according to him, manifests that the bar is qualified by the words in contravention of any other law. Mr Islam contended that if such transfer by way of sale, gift, mortgage, exchange or lease for a period exceeding 5 years is barred by any existing law in force then notwithstanding the previous sanction of the Administrator, the transfer would be invalid. He has referred the cases of State of Rajasthan vs Sripal Jain, AIR 1963 SC 1323 and Rohit Pulp and Paper Mills Ltd. vs Collector of Central Excise, Baroda, (1990) 3 SCC 447 in support of his contention. According to Mr Islam, the words used in both sections are clear enough to come to the conclusion that there is no scope to give any statutory interpretation by restricting the power of the Waqfs Administrator. Mr Islam finally contended that the generic words used in section 33 should receive a limited interpretation by reason of its context by legitimately drawing upon the noscitur a sociis principle. In the other words, it is submitted that the restricted words used in the section should be interpreted by applying the principle of 'noscitur a sociis' or on the analogy of the 'ejusdem generis' principle

11. In the case of Rohit Pulp and Paper Mills Ltd., the assessee has a factory in which different variety of paper and paper boards are being manufactured. Paper and paper board' are goods falling under Item 17(1) of the Central Excise and Salt Act, 1944. Two notifications were issued one on March, 1984 in respect of the above Item providing 10% ad valorem paper plus Rs 1005 per metric tonne. Second notification provides for a concession in respect of paper and paper boards falling under Item 17(1) of the schedule manufactured out of pulp containing not less than 50% by weight of pulp made from materials other than bamboo and cleared on or after April 1st, 1944, at the rate of Rs 450 per metric tonne. The above concessional rates were subject to certain conditions set up in the proviso to the notification stating that the exemption contained in the notification shall not apply to cigarette tissue, glassine paper, coated paper (including waxed paper) and so on. The assessee initially paid excise duty as per previous notification but later on it claimed confessional rate prescribed by the latter notification. The Excise Department refused to permit the assessee to avail this concession in respect of his manufactured goods. It claimed concessional rates on the ground that the word 'coated paper' has been set out in the proviso along with other 4 items and used in wider sense and includes coated papers of all varities, it should be interpreted by applying the principle of 'noscitur a sociis' or on the analogy of 'ejusdem generis' principle.

12. The Supreme Court accepted the claim holding that there is no reason why rationally logical restriction should not be placed in the proviso based on the classification and that coated paper in the second proviso refers only to coated paper used for industrial purposes and not to coated varieties of printing and writing paper" and in the context with which we can legimately draw upon the noscitur a sociis principle.

13. In State of Bombay vs Hospital Mazdoor  Savha, AIR 1960 SC 610, the question involved was that two employees of a chain of hospitals were removed and in their place two state servants were appointed. The retrenched employees filed a writ of mandamus directing to rein-statement in their posts on the ground that the retrenchment was void as it did not comply the provisions of sections 25F and 25H of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The petition was resisted on the ground that the writ petition was not maintainable, inasmuch as, the hospitals did not constitute an 'industry' and so, the relevant provisions of law were not applicable. The question involved in the appeal for consideration is whether group of hospitals constitutes an 'industry'. The writ petition was ultimately allowed on the reasoning that the orders had not complied the mandatory provisions of law. On appeal from the said judgment it was raised that the definition of 'industry' defined in section 2(j) of the said Act is so wide denotation, 'hospitals' can be excluded from the definition. It was urged that in construing the definition, the Court must adopt the rule of construction 'noscuntur a sociis'.

14. Gajendragadkar, J. upon consideration of the opinions expressed by different authors on Interpretation of Statutes came to the conclusion that the maxim 'noscuntur a sociis' is merely a rule of construction and it cannot prevail in cases where it is clear that the wider words have been deliberately used in order to make the scope of the defined word correspondingly wider. It is only where the intention of the Legislature in associating wider words with words of narrower significance is doubtful, or otherwise not clear that the present rule of construction can be usefully applied. It can also be applied where the meaning of the words of wider import is doubtful; but where the object of the Legislature, in using wider words, is clear and free of ambiguity, the rule of construction in question cannot be pressed into service".

15. 'Noscitur a sociis' is a Latin maxim which means that it is known by its associates. To say more clearly, the meaning of a word is to be judged by the company it keeps. It is a rule laid down by Lord Bacon that the coupling of words together shows that they are to be under-stood in the same sense. Where the meaning of a particular word is doubtful or obscure, or where a particular expression taken singly is inoperative, the intention of the Legislature may be ascertained by looking at adjoining words, or at expressions occurring in other parts of the same statute. One provision of the statute must be construed by the bearing it will have upon another (Latin for Lawyers, 31C Edn. page 195). 16. In this connection the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Attorney-General for Ortario vs Mercer, (J.yy3) AC 767 (778) said It is a sound, maxim of law that every word in a statute ought prima-facie to be construed in its primary and natural sense, unless a secondary or more limited sense is required by the subject or the context. Whether there is a particular description of objects, sufficient to identify what was intended, followed by general or omnibus description, the latter description will be confined to the objects of the same class or kind of the former. This rule is not applicable in this case, inasmuch as, the philosophy of this rule is applied in cases when the meaning of a doubtful word may be ascertained by reference to the meaning of words associated with it. When two or more words which are susceptible of analogous meaning, the more general is restricted to a sense analogous to a less general.

17. The efusdern generis rule is a particular application of the broader maxim 'noscitur a sociis' principle. The difference between these two rules as explained in Words and Phrases Vol. XIV, page 207, is thus: Associated words take their meaning from one another under the doctrine of noscitur a sociis, the philosophy of which is that the meaning of a doubtful word may be ascertained by reference to the meaning of words associated with it; such doctrine is broader than the maxim ejusdem generis. The ejusdem generis rule has been clearly explained in a New Zealand case in Cooney, (1901) 21 NZLR 106 (108) by William, J. thus:

"There is a very well known rule of construction that if a general word follows a particular and specific word of the same nature as itself, it takes its meaning from that word, and is presumed to be restricted to the same genus as that word. No doubt that rule is one which has to be followed with care; but if not to follow it leads to absurd results, then it ought to be followed",

18. This doctrine, according to Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes, 12th Edn. P. 289 means that, where two or more words which are susceptible of analogous meaning are coupled together they are understood to be used in their cognate sense. They take as it were their colour from each other, i.e. the more general is restricted to a sense analogous to a less general. Lord Campbell in RV. Edmundson (1859) 28 WC 213 explained this rule by saying accede to the principle laid down in all the cases which have been cited, that, where there are general words following particular and specific words, the general words must be confirmed to things of the same kind as those specified.

19. In dealing with wider words in the con-text of the ejusdem generis rule, Lord Bramwell in Great Western RY. vs Sarindon Ry, (1884) 9 AC 786 said "As a matter of ordinary construction where several words are followed by a general expression which is as much applicable to the first and other words as to the last, that expression is not limited to the last applies to all. For instance, horses, oxen, pigs, and sheep, from whatever country they may come the latter words would apply to horses as much as to sheep. The ejusdem generis rule according to Craies on Statute Law, Seventh Edition, is one to be applied with caution and not pushed too far, as in the case of many discussions, which treat it as automatically applicable, not as being, what it is, a mere presumption, in the absence of other indications of the intention of the Legislature. In NAIGOV Bolton Corporation, (1943) AC 166, Lord Wright said, The ejusdem generis nile is often useful or convenient, but it is merely a rule of construction, not a rule of law.

20. The position has been summed up in Halsbury's Laws of England, 3rd Edn, page 397 thus: "As a rule, where a statute there are general words following particular and specific words, the general words must be confined to things of the same kind as those specified, although this, as a rule of construction, must be applied with caution, and subject to the primary rule that statutes are to be constructed in accordance with the intention of the parliament. For the ejusdem rule to apply, the specific words must constitute a category, class or genus; if they constitute such a category, class or genus; then only things which belong to that category, class or genus fall within the general words".

21. According to the established principle of interpretation of statutes, the specific words must apply not to different objects of a widely differing character but to something which can be called a class or kind of object. Where this is lacking the rule cannot apply. Where the words are clearly wide in their meaning they ought not to be qualified on the ground of their association with other words. So, general words following particular words will not include anything of a class superior to that to which the particular words belong. In cases where there is no doubt that the wider words have been deliberately used in order to make the scope of the defined words correspondingly wider, where the intention of the legislature in associating wider words with words of narrower significance is used is doubtful, the above rule of construction can be used. It is the established rule of construction that the statutes are to be construed in accordance with the intention of the Legislature.

22. On a plain reading of section 56 we find no ambiguity in the language used therein with the language used in section 33 of the Ordinance. There is no doubt on reading section 33 as a whole about the meaning of the words used therein which can be ascertained by reference to the meaning of words associated with it. Therefore, we need not draw upon the noscitur a sociis is or ejusdem generis principles. Section 33 restricts the Administrator in transferring any part of a waqf property while he is in charge of the said property. He can transfer the property for the welfare of the estate with prior permission of the Government. Whereas, the substance of sub-section (1) of section 56 is that a mutawalli can transfer any part of a waqf property in any manner as provided therein but the only restriction is in respect of lease for a period exceeding five years. In such case previous permission of the Waqfs Administrator is necessary. Even if any transfer by way of lease is made for a period exceeding five years with-out sanction of the Administrator, such transfer can be declared void by the Civil Court only on the prayer of the Administrator. Sub-section (4) makes the thing more clear, which provides that even if a mutawalli transfers any property in contravention of sub-section (1) and afterwards he becomes the owner of the property, he may re-convey the property on the direction of the Administrator. It is also provided in sub-section (5) that if any transfer is made in contravention of sub-section (1), such transfer shall be deemed to be an act of malfeasance.

23. If the object and purpose of section 56 are considered together, there would be no difficulty in holding that the words of wide import have been deliberately used by the Legislature in the exercise of powers by the mutawalli to transfer any part of the waqf property by way of lease exceeding 5 years with the sanction of the Administrator. Section 33 empowers the Administrator any sort of transfer of any portion of the Waqf Property with previous sanction of the Government, whereas, in case of transfer by mutawalli other than lease not exceeding 5 years previous sanction of the Administrator is not necessary. There is no ambiguity in the words used in those provisions. There cannot be any doubt of using wider words in section 56(1) and the intention of the Legislature in using wider words is clear and free from any ambiguity. These two provisions would be realized if we bear in mind the scheme of Chapters III and VI. The intention of the Legislature in providing these two provisions in different chapters is clear. On a plain reading of section 56 it suggests that it would be inappropriate to put a restrictive interpretation.

24. In the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 56, it is stated that even if there is previous sanction such transfer shall not be validated if it is in contravention of any other law, that is, if any other law prohibits such transfer, any lease exceeding five years even with the previous sanction of the Administrator shall be invalid. Now it is to be looked into whether the lease in question has been granted in violation of any existing law, that is, the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 (Act, 1949) and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act, 1950). The answer to this point depends upon the determination of the nature of the land transferred and the application of those laws in the context of the execution of the deed in question. Admittedly, the suit land is situated within Sylhet City Corporation area and the nature of the suit land has been mentioned as (Bangla) (vegetable garden). Thus the suit land is non-agricultural land. 'Non-agricultural land' within section 2(4) of the Act, 1949 means "land which is used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture and includes any land which is held on lease for the purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture irrespective of whether it is used for any such purpose......

25. A land which was originally leased for agricultural or horticultural purposes but is being used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture without the consent of the landlord and if the period for which the land has been so used is less than twelve years will not be included in the category of 'non-agricultural land' in view of section 2(4)(b). This exception is not applicable to this case in view of the admitted fact that the lease was granted not for a period less than twelve years. So the primary test in determining a particular land is non-agricultural or not, rests firstly as to whether the land is a 'non-agricultural land' as defined in the Act of 1949, and secondly, the purpose for which the tenancy was created.

<u>26. This definition excludes agricultural and horticultural lands including the lands held in lease for purposes not connected with agriculture and horticulture. The land is in the nature of horticulture but the lease deed does not show that the lease was granted for horticulture purposes. It means that the land which is used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture and includes any land which is held on lease for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture irrespective of whether it is used for any such purposes or not is non-agricultural land. There are two classes of non-agricultural tenants under the said Act, namely (a) tenants, and (b) under-tenants. 'Non-agricultural tenant' within the meaning of section 2(5) of Act, 1949 is a person who holds non-agricultural land under another person with consent of that person and is, or but for a special contract would be, liable to pay rent to such person for that land. In the Act of 1950, almost similar definition has been given in section 2(17). Under this Act, a tenant who holds land for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture, but does not include a person holding land together with any building standing thereon and necessary adjuncts thereto under a lease other than a lease in perpetuity.</u>

27. The difference under these two enactments is that if any person holds any premises on such land under a contract to pay rent for such occupation such person shall riot become a 'non-agricultural tenant' under the Act of 1949 and secondly, a lease in perpetuity has been excluded from the category in the latter Act. According to section 1(2) of the Act of 1949 the word 'tenant' means a person who has acquired from the proprietor or a tenure holder a right to hold non-agricultural land for any of the purposes provided in the said Act, and includes also the successors-in-interest of persons who have acquired such a right. Under the latter Act, tenant means a person who holds land under another person and is, or but for a special contract would be, liable to pay for that land to that person. Under the definition a 'borga cultivator' is excluded from the category of tenant. Under-tenant as per sub-section (3) of section 3 of Act;, 1949 means a person who has acquired a right to hold non-agricultural land for any of the purposes provided in the Act either immediately or under a tenant and includes also the successors-in-interest of per-sons who have acquired such a right.

28. The defendant's tenancy was created after the Act of 1949 came into force in 1965, and therefore, he was an under-tenant within the meaning of Act, 1949 during the relevant times. Section 4 provided the purpose for which a non-agricultural tenant may hold non-agricultural land i.e. for (a) homestead or residential purposes; (b) manufacturing or business purposes; or (c) religious or other purposes. The word 'homestead' includes gardens, tanks and land necessary for enjoyment as home-stead. Under section 2(14) of the Act, 1950, the word 'homestead' means a dwelling house with the land under it, together with any court-yard, garden, tank, place of worship and private burial or cremation ground attached and appertaining to such dwelling house, and includes any out-buildings used for the purpose of enjoying the dwelling house or for purposes connected with agricultural or horticulture and such lands within well-defined limits, whether vacant or not, as are treated to be appertaining thereto.

29. The expression 'other purposes' used in clause (c) of section 4 of Act, 1949 means purposes other than non-agricultural and horticulture. The courts below on construction of the lease deed came to a definite finding that the lease was granted in perpetuity. Provisions have been made for the protection of under-tenants in Chapter IV of Act, 1949. Section 20 provides that an under-tenant shall be liable to ejectment on two grounds namely (a) if he has used the land in a manner which renders it unfit for use for any of the purposes specified in section 4, and (b) the term of the lease has expired when he holds the non-agricultural under a written lease. There is no allegation that the defendant has been using the land in contravention of section 4. Since the lease is in perpetuity, clause (b) of section 20 is not also applicable in this case.

30. Other protections given to an under-tenant are those provided in sections 21 and 22. Section 21 recognizes the succession by the heirs of 'under-tenant' in case of his death subject to the provisions of sections 90 and 91 of the Act, 1950. These provisions are also not applicable in this case. Section 22 recognizes all rights and liabilities of a tenant as set forth in sections 7, 8 and 10. If the term is not less than twelve years specified in the lease deed and in that case, section 6 shall apply and also section 20 in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of section 22 shall not apply. Section 6 provides the manner of use of non-agricultural land by a tenant.

31. Since there is no allegation of violation of section 6 no discussion on this provision is called for. Section 7 provides the rights and liabilities of the tenants in respect of a tenancy created before or after the commencement of the Transfer of Property Act, and in case of a lease created in writing for a period not less than twelve years, and if the landlord has allowed the tenant to raise constructions or structures before the expiry period of lease, then the ten-ant holding the non-agricultural land shall not be ejected by the landlord on any grounds other than for the purposes specified in the section. In case of death of the tenant his heirs shall inherit the tenanted property. These protections provided to an under-tenant in Chapter IV would be applicable to the defendant if section 26A had not been inserted in the Act of 1949 in 1967 but the scenario has totally been changed after the amendment.

32. Section 23 of the Act provides the manner of transfer of non-agricultural land. It is provided that every transfer of the non-agricultural land by a non-agricultural tenant shall be made by registered instrument. The lease in question was executed by a registered instrument and thus, the lease satisfied the requirements of section 23. There is another aspect which is very much important for resolving the dispute in controversy. After the acquisition of rent receiving interest, there was restriction for sub-letting of any land by section 75A of the Act, 1950 which was inserted by Act XII of 1954. Under this provision the creation of a subordinate tenancy was prohibited and/or invalidated. Under the amendment the rent-receivers were themselves to retain certain classes of retainable khas land as tenant directly under the Government. They were restricted to create further sub-tenancies under them. The creation of sub-tenancy was validated which were effected before the publication of the Notification under sections 17(3) or 31(1) of the said Act. Similar prohibition for sub-letting has been provided in section 26A (1) of Act, 1949 by the East Pakistan Ordinance No. IX of 1967, which provides, Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, no non-agricultural tenant shall sub-let the whole or any part of his tenancy on any terms or conditions whatsoever.

33. All rent receiving interests of persons who have been described as 'rent-receivers', in clause (23) of section 2 in Act, 1950 i.e. the rent receiving interest of (i) proprietors, (ii) tenure-holders, (iii) raiyats, (iv) under-raiyats, (v) non-agriculture tenants, when a non-agricultural tenant has let out non-agricultural lands, and (vi) landlords in respect of service-tenures have been acquired by the Government. What can-not be acquired under the Act of 1950 are non-rent receiving interests in respect of non-agricultural land with building standing thereon together with necessary adjuncts held under a lease not being a lease in perpetuity as per clauses (17) and (23) of section 2; portion in hats and bazaars which do not fall within the definition of hat or bazaar and having structure and held under lease; khas lands to the extent of 100 standard bighas; khas lands in excess of the above limit where a rent-receiver, cultivating raiyat or cultivating under-raiyat has or have undertaken large-scale farming, dairy-farming duly certified by the Revenue Authority; lands held for the purpose of cultivation and manufacture of tea or coffee or for cultivation of rubber if certified by the Revenue Authority; land covered by buildings or structures and necessary adjuncts thereto in case of any large scale industry, and land held under waqf or debutter when incomes from such property are wholly applied to religious or charitable purposes in view of section 20(5) (i)(c) and (ii) of Act, 1950.

34. A rent receiver within the meaning of section 2(23) of Act, 1950 includes a proprietor or a tenure-holder and a raiyat, underraiyat or a non-agricultural tenant whose land has been let out and also the immediate landlord of a person who holds any land free of rent in consideration of some service to be rendered. Therefore, we find that a non-aquiculture ten-ant has been included in the category of a rent-receiver in the said Act. In the Act, 1949, the expression 'raiyat' or 'rent-receiver' has not been used or defined and in its place, the term a 'tenant' or an 'under-tenant' has been used. On a combined reading of these provisions, we find that the expressions of "raiyat" or a "tenant" are genus and an under-raiyat' or a 'sub-tenant' or an 'under-tenant' are species. The rent receiving interest of a raiyat passes to the Government after the acquisition of receiving interest and the rent-receiver accrued the right to receive compensation. Similarly a tenant under the Act of 1949 becomes a rent-receiver when his land has been let out to another per-son who holds it on a contract to pay rent after section 26A comes into effect.

35. Next the question to be considered is whether in view of section 70 of Act, 1949, the defendant can be evicted by the plaintiff in execution of a decree of civil Court. Section 70 pro-vides non-agricultural tenant shall be ejected from the tenancy or from any non-agricultural land which he holds except in execution of a decree of a competent civil Court". This provision clearly suggests that a non-agricultural tenant can be evicted by the landlord through a decree of a civil Court. This section is in part materia with section 89 of Bengal Tenancy Act. The effect of this section is to limit the landlord the right of ejectment under the Act. This section was in existence in the original Act of 1949 with a view to protect the tenants from being evicted by the landlords from non-agricultural land other than by due process of law. This section becomes obsolete after section 26A has come into force.

36. Section 83 of Act, 1950 provides that a raiyat shall have the right to occupy and use the land comprised in his holding in any manner he likes. With the acquisition of lands of different classes of rent receivers, rent receiving interest extends up to the end of Part IV. The second division starts with Part V and extends upto the end of Act, 1950. Different provisions of Part V became operative in different areas or districts from the date of publication of notifications and thereupon Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed on those areas or districts. All holders of land within the areas in respect of which compensation assessment-roll has been published, became tenants under the Government. Section 81A of Act, 1950 provides rights and liabilities of non-agricultural tenants. It says;

"(1) Except as otherwise provided in this Part, the rights and liabilities a holder of non-agricultural land, who has become a tenant under the Government in respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior right in such-land under the pro-visions of this Act, shall, where the provisions of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, applied to such land, at the time of such acquisition, be regulated by provisions of that Act.

(2) The rights and liabilities of other non-agricultural tenants shall, except in the matter of determination, enhancement or reduction of rent, be governed by the terms of the lease and the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882."

37. This section 81A has been inserted by the East Pakistan Ordinance No.VIII of 1967 simultaneously on the same day the Ordinance No. IX of 1967 was inserted in the Act of 1949. Section 81A says that the rights and liabilities of a tenant under the Government with regard to his non-agricultural land shall be governed by the provisions of Act, 1949 and the rights and liabilities of other non-agricultural tenants i.e. excluding tenants with regard to non-agricultural land envisaged in sub-section (1) of section 81A shall be governed by the Transfer of Property Act "except in the matter of determination, enhancement or reduction of rent". With regard to these excepted matters the Act of 1950 will, of course be applicable. The proviso to section 81A puts an embargo on non-agricultural tenant against sub-letting of non-agricultural land containing a provision of forfeiture in case of breach of this prohibition.

38. Section 81 of Act, 1950 says that after coming into force of Part V in any area, there shall be only one class of holders of agricultural land, namely, 'maliks'. Section 82 (2) also contains in Part V of Act, 1950 which defines the word "raiyat", means a person who, by virtue of section 44 or otherwise, has acquired a right to hold land directly under the Government mainly for the purpose of cultivating it by him-self or by members of his family or by, or with the aid of, servants or laborer or with the aid of partner or borgader, and includes also the successor-in-interest of persons who had acquired such right. According to sub-section (8) of section 82, on and from the date on which Part V comes into effect in any area, the word "malik" shall be deemed to have been substituted for the word "raiyat" or "tenant", and the word "land revenue" shall stand for the word 'rent'.

39. If a non-agricultural tenant sub-lets his tenancy or a part thereof in contravention of subsection (1), the tenancy shall be extinguished and shall vest in the Government as per sub-section (2) of section 26A. When the lease under consideration was created this pro-vision was nonexistent. As observed above, the defendant was an under-tenant when the tenancy was created. Now the question for consideration is to determine the status of the defendant after insertion of section 26A. On a combined reading of sections 81 and 82(8), there is no gainsaying that a sub-tenant or under-tenant created by a tenant has matured his status as a tenant/malik under the Act of 1949 on and from the date of section 26A coming into force. 40. In Province of East Pakistan vs Muhammad Hossain, 16 DLR (SC) 667, the question arose for consideration was whether after the acquisition of rent receiving interest, a tenancy created by a rent-receiver in respect Of non-agricultural land is hit by section 75A or in the alternative there is conflict between section 9 and 75A of the Act. It was observed by H. Rahman, J. 'Section 75A, though it came into force on the 30th August 1954, was made operative only from the date or notification under section 11 (3) or section 31 (1) and, as such, it had no retrospective operation and did not invalidate leases created before such date." Similar principle will be applicable to the case of defendant whose lease was created prior to the insertion of section 26A.

41. Section 26(2)(a) explained the word 'transfer' used in section 23 of Act, 1949. It says, "transfer" does not include partition or a sub lease or until, a decree or order absolute for foreclosure is made, simple or usufructory mortgage or mortgage by conditional sale. The words 'or a sub-lease' were deleted by Ordinance IX of 1967. Though in the original Act, 1944 a sub-lease was not treated as 'transfer', the defendant having continued as tenant in the suit land in the same manner even after the amendment, his lease in respect of the suit land has become 'transfer' within the meaning of the Act of 1949.

42. The purpose of omitting the word 'sub-lease' by Ordinance IX of 1967 as evident is only for the purpose of avoiding preemption under section 24 of the Act. In the said Act the word 'sub-let' has not been defined. Only the word 'under-tenant' has been defined in section 3(3). The use of the expression 'sublet' in my view is misnomer, inasmuch as, if we read this provision along with sections 3, 21 and 22, the intention of the Legislature will be discernible. The expression 'sub-lease' or 'sublet' have been used in the same context of the term 'under-tenant' and they are used in cognate sense. A sub-ordinate tenancy under which an under-tenant would be liable to pay for that land to a person other than the Government is liable pay to the Government after section 26A came into force and his status has been upgraded to a tenant/malik. In other words, after insertion of section 26A by Ordinance No.IX of 1967, there is one category of non-agricultural tenant on and from 22nd December, 1967 and the defendant is a tenant/malik under the Government and whatever right the plaintiff had in respect of the suit land extinguished from that date. Thus, there is no violation of section 26A or any other provisions of the Act, 1949 or Act, 1950. Now the rights which have been given to a raiyat under section 83 of the Act, 1950 can also be exercised by a under-tenant created before 1967, such as, to occupy and use the non-agricultural land in any manner he likes.

43. As noticed above, in the definition of 'non-agricultural tenant', a lease in perpetuity has been excluded from the category of non-agricultural tenant. Since the status of the defendant has become a tenant/malik within the meaning of section 3(2) of the Act, 1949 and section 2(27) of the Act, 1950, on and from 22nd December, 1967, the ex-landlord, i.e. the plaintiff has no locus-standi to maintain the suit as framed in view of the fact that whatever right or interest he had in the suit land had ceased to exist after section 26A came into force. Moreso, the trial Court after the construction of the lease deed and other evidence on record held that the lease was acted upon as it was created by a registered deed followed by the delivery of possession, mutation of the name of the defendant and the payment of rent to the Government and those findings having been maintained by the High Court Division observing that the trial Court was justified in arriving at such conclusion, the suit as framed is not maintainable as the same is barred by section 42 of-the Specific Relief Act.

44. Mr Bhuiyan contended that even if it is assumed that the Administrator accorded sanction, such sanction was obtained mechanically without holding any inquiry and giving notice to the persons affected by the transfer and also without hearing the parties and as such, the sanction is not a sanction in the eye of law. Therefore, the lease, according to him, is violative to section 57 of the Waqfs Ordinance. This point is devoid of substance, inasmuch as, neither in the plaint nor at any stage of the proceeding the plaintiff has raised this point. The learned counsel has raised this point for the first time before this Division. If such point had been raised at the initial stage of the proceedings, the defendant would have been able to prove that the lease was granted following the procedures by calling the record from the office of the Waqfs Administrator. Moreso, in the recital of the deed there are averments that as the residential houses of the Waqf Estate were in a dilapidated condition and could not be repaired due to shortage of fund, the land was leased out for the welfare of the Waqf Estate with prior sanction the Waqfs Administrator. Therefore, the lease was granted for the benefit and welfare of the Waqf Estate and also for the purpose of fulfilling the objects for which the waqf was created.

<u>45. An Administrator is appointed by the Government in exercise of powers conferred under section 7 of the Waqfs Ordinance. Section 10 of the Ordinance states that the Administrator shall be deemed to be a public officer with-in the meaning of the Code of Civil Procedure. Naturally he is a public servant and he has accorded the sanction while discharging public duties as a public servant. There is presumption of regularity of the official acts by a person in discharge of his official duty until the contrary is proved. The court, in the absence of anything to the contrary, may presume that such permission was accorded after holding a proper inquiry in accordance with law. Over and above, since the plaintiff has no right or interest in the suit land, he has no locus standi to raise question about the legality of the lease.</u>

46. Now turning to the merit of the case, it appears that the trial Court on assessment of the evidence on record held that the lease deed was executed in accordance with law which was legal; that the plaintiff's predecessor Ashid Ullah handed over possession of the suit land after the execution of the deed; that the plaintiff failed to prove the manner of his possession of the suit land after the death of his father; that the plaintiff did not acquire title in the suit land; that the defendant proved that he is in possession of the suit land, but that he failed to prove his possession in respect of the entire suit land and that the lease was acted upon. The ambiguity in the finding of trial Court is in respect of the possession followed by dispossession. In order to remove this anomaly, the High Court Division remanded Title Suit No. 38 of 1992 to the trial Court for fresh decision on this point. The Court of Appeal below alter the remand came to a definite finding that the plaintiff dispossessed the defendant in respect of only 0.03 acre of land.

47. The Court of Appeal while disposing of the original appeals arose out of the suits observed that lease having been granted in perpetuity with the right of inheritance on the death of the defendant and also with the power to transfer, it was created in the similar manner as the Landlords used to settle lands by pattas before the Act, 1950 came into force. Such transfer is not permissible in that in case of lease, no ownership is transferred. It is further observed that a Lease for a limited period can be made but after the expiry of the period, such lease can be extended for the purpose of enjoyment of the land and that in case of violation of the terms, the lease can be cancelled without service of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act.

<u>48. These findings are based on misconception of law. The Court of Appeal below misconstrued section 56 of the Ordinance in assuming that a mutawalli cannot grant lease of any part of waqf property in perpetuity with prior sanction of the Administrator. The language used in this section is so explicit that the mutawalli can exercise the right of transfer by way of lease for a period exceeding 5 years with prior approval of the Administrator. There is no prohibition either directly or impliedly to create such a lease. The words and figure 'exceeding 5 years' are wide enough to infer to any period. There is no scope to read the word 'exceeding' in a narrower sense like 'otherwise than in perpetuity' in view of the fact that if we read the words 'by way of sale' with the words and figure 'by way of lease for a term exceeding 5 years', there is no doubt that the intention of the Legislature is wide enough to infer a transfer by way of lease in perpetuity. The words or by way of lease for a term exceeding 5 years shall be void' used after 'comma' before the word 'exchange' are clear enough to arrive at a conclusion that the mutawalli can transfer by way of lease of the nature provided he had obtained previous sanction of the Administrator.</u>

49. The Court of Appeal below committed another fundamental error in assuming that no lease of immovable property could be granted other than a lease for occupation of the land for a limited period. Further, the Court of Appeal below compared creation of the tenancy with the settlement of land made by ex-landlords under the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1985 on a misconception of law. The Court of Appeal below ought to have ascertained the nature of the land, the laws applicable to such lease and the construction of the deed before deciding the question on whether the mutawalli of a waqf estate has power, to transfer a portion of the waqf property by way of lease for a period exceeding 5 years. As observed above, the lease was created in respect of non-agricultural land. A tenant holding non-agricultural land under a lease in writing for a period exceeding twelve years shall not be ejected by the landlord on any grounds other than the grounds specified in section 4 of Act 1949 and his interest shall, in case of death, be devolved upon his heirs in view of clauses (i) and (ii) respectively of sub-section (3) of section 7. Similarly in case of a tenancy created to an 'under-tenant' corresponding rights of protection have been given be sections 20, 21 and 22 of the Act, 1949.

50. The Court of Appeal below committed further error by treating the questioned lease similar to one of cases not governed by a contract or local law or usage. Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act applies to a case whether no period of lease is agreed between the parties or whether the lease being unregistered cannot be looked at to ascertain the agreed period. Finally, it has committed another fundamental error in assuming that a mutawalli can grant only such nature of lease of immovable property the rescission of which does not require service of notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The Court of Appeal below failed to notice that a lease of immovable property cannot be determined by either parties without due service of notice. As to the duration of a lease, a statutory presumption is permitted.

51. In the case of leases for agricultural or manufacturing purposes, the presumption will be that they are from year to year and in the case of other leases the tenancy is deemed to be from month to month. In the former case a six month's notice is necessary for terminating lease and in the latter case fifteen days notice is necessary. These provisions are quite distinguishable and not applicable to the case of the defendant in view of the discussions made above. The Court of Appeal below approached the matter on wrong premise in considering the lease in question and such wrong approach had reflected in the latter part of the judgment. It has not explained why a lease of non-agricultural land granted with prior sanction of the Administrator in respect of any part of Waqf property by the mutawalli for the welfare of the waqf estate would be illegal. The High Court Division on consideration of section 56 of the Ordinance has rightly approved the views of the trial Court. The High Court Division held that the lease having been created with prior sanction of the Administrator was legal and valid. Accordingly, the High Court Division has rightly found that the plaintiff's suit is not maintainable and is liable to be dismissed.

65. In support of his contentions Mr Bhuiyan has referred to the cases of AK Gopalan vs State of Madras AIR 1950, SC 27 and Hafizuddin Ahmed vs M Aslam Minh, 55 DLR 95.

66. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Counsel, appearing on behalf of the respondents, on the other hand, has submitted that the learned Judge of the Single Bench correctly interpreted the provisions of section 56 of the Ordinance in holding that the Appellate Court was wrong in holding that the lease for a term exceeding 5(five) years even with sanction of the Administrator of Waqfs could not be valid and in restoring those of the trial Court. He, by referring to the issues framed in the suits and the findings of the trial Court, has further submitted that in none of the suits, any issue as to the non-sufficiency of the inquiry or non-holding of enquiry by the Administrator of Waqfs as required under section of the Ordinance before giving sanction to the mutawalli to lease out the land in question was suggested or raised, the appellant is not entitled to raise the issue before this Court for the first time. Mr Mahabubey Alam has lastly submitted, that the lessee duly paid the Nazrana and the rent to the lessor and he was delivered possession of the leasehold land and thus the lease was acted upon, the trial Court rightly dismissed the suit, but the Appellate Court though the final Court of fact approached the case from a wrong stand point in taking converse view on total misinterpretation of the provisions of section 56 of the Ordinance and thus erred in law in decreeing Title Suit No. 26 of 1992 and the High Court Division rightly interfered with the same and as such, the impugned judgment and order does not call for any interference by this Court and the appeal be dismissed.

67. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel who was appointed as amicus curiae, has submitted that to interpret a statute or law other accompanying words are to be read together. Mr. Islam by invoking the rule of "noscitur a sociis" has submitted that if the other accompanying words of section 56(1) before the words "or by way of lease for a term exceeding 5 years shall be valid without the previous sanction of the Administrator" are read together it would appear that the legislature has not put any bar to transfer any immovable property of a waqf by way of lease for a period exceeding 5 (five) years with the previous sanction of the Administrator of Waqfs. In support of his submission Mr. Islam has referred to the case of Rohit Pulp and Paper Mills Ltd vs Collector of Central Excise Baroda, Supreme Court Cases, 1990 Vol. III, 447.

68. Let us examine the submissions of the learned Counsel of the respective parties and the learned amicus curiae in the light of the pleadings of the parties, the findings given by the Courts below and the relevant; provisions of the Ordinance.

69. From the judgment of the trial Court, it appears that though both suits were disposed of by a common judgment, it decided the merit of the suit separately and decided the merit of Title Suit No. 26 of 1992 first. The trial Court dismissed Title Suit No.26 of 1992 on the finding, inter alia, that (i) defendant No.1 (plaintiff of Title Suit No.38 of 1992) got possession of the lease hold land from the lessor pursuant to the lease deed dated 18-5-1965. In coming to the said finding the trial Court considered the kabala dated 21-12-1965 being No.5384, exhibit-K(1) by which defendant No.1 purchased 4 (four) decimals of land from the adjacent plot being plot number 933, rent receipts: exhibits-'Kha and Kha(1)' by which he paid rents in respect of the land in question upto 1379-1382 and exhibit- 'Ga' the certified copies of the order sheets of the mutation proceedings, (ii) the lease deed of defendant No.1 dated 18-5-1965 is valid and is in existence and he produced sufficient documentary evidence in sup-port of his claim of acquisition of title in the leasehold land, (iii) The plaintiff failed to prove his title and possession in the second schedule land, (iv) the defendant acquired his valid title in the second schedule land by virtue of the lease deed dated 18-5-1965 and he is in possession thereof, but not in its entire area and he also failed to prove his possession in any particular direction (in Bangla it has been stat এবং তাহার দখল কোন দিকে আছে তাহা সুনির্দিষ্ট ভাবে প্রমানিত হয় নাই।) (v) The plaintiff failed to prove his possession in the second schedule land, so he was not entitled to get the decree as prayed for and (vi) the suit was barred by limitation and was also not maintainable in its present form.

70. Title Suit No. 38 of 1992 was dismissed with the finding, inter alin, that (i) the suit was filed within time, (ii) the suit was maintainable, (iii) there was no defect of party in framing the suit and (iv) the plaintiff was not entitled to the decree as prayed for as he failed to prove his exclusive possession in the specific, area of the first schedule land excluding the second schedule land though he proved his title therein.

<u>71. From the judgment of the Appellate Court, it appears that it allowed Title Appeal No.57 of 1995 (this appeal was filed against the judgment and decreed passed in Title Suit No.26 of 1992) on the view that section 56 of the Ordinance did not authorise the mutawalli of a waqf estate to lease out its immovable property permanently. The Appellate Court further held that though exhibit-'Kha' showed that the Administrator of Waqfs gave sanction to the then mutawalli-Asidullah, the father of the plaintiff to lease out the land in question of the waqf permanently, the Administrator of Waqf had no power to give such sanction under section 56 of the Ordinance. The Appellate Court further held that the defendant failed to file any receipt showing payment of rent to the waqf estate and by mutating his name as apparent from exhibit-'Kha', he did not acquire any title to the lease hold land and the evidence adduced by the defendant as to his possession in the said land and then dispossession from the second schedule land did not prove his exclusive possession therein.</u>

72. As stated earlier, the High Court Division sent Title Suit No.38 of 1992 back on remand to the trial Court for writing out a fresh judgment on the question of possession and dispossession only as made out by the plaintiff in the plaint in the light of the observations made in the judgment. From the impugned judgment and order, it appears that about the finding of possession of the trial Court as well as the Appellate Court, the High Court Division observed as follows: "with regard to possession, the trial Court appears to have considered the oral evidence and came to a finding that 'opposite party No.1 failed to prove his possession and that the petitioner was in possession in one part of his judgment but at the conclusion it held the possession of the petitioner was not definitely and clearly proved. Upon such view, the trial Court dismissed the suit of the petitioner. Appellate Court appears to have considered no oral evidence at all. The conclusion of the appellate court on possession is influenced by its wrong decision on the deed of lease. Such finding on possession based on total 'non-reading of the evidence oral and documentary on record cannot also be sustained in law."

73. From the documents incorporated in the paper book of Leave Petition No.1568 of 2007, it appears that pursuant to the direction given in the impugned judgment and order in connection with Civil Revision No.2572 of 1998 the Joint District Judge on re-hearing Title Suit No. 38 of 1992 by judgment and decree dated the 10th day of September, 2002 dismissed the suit again. Against the said judgment and decree of the Joint District Judge, the plaintiff filed Title Appeal No. 197 of 2002 before the District Judge, Sylhet. The appeal was allowed in part by the learned Additional District Judge, first Court, Sylhet in the following terms:

"That the appeal be partly allowed on contest against the defendant-respondent No.1 and ex-parte against the rest without costs. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Court below are hereby set aside. The plaintiff-appellants' title over the suit land is hereby declared. The appellants' prayer for recovery of khas possession against the defendant-respondents in respect of 0.03 decimals of land is also allowed. The defendant-respondents are hereby directed to vacate the said land and deliver the possession of the same to the plaintiff appellants by peaceful means as stated in the 2nd schedule of the plaint within 90(Ninety) days from the date of this orders, violation of which shall be seriously dealt with in accordance with law. At the same time, the plaintiff appellants after the expiry of those days, could recover the khas possession of the same by the aid and assistance of the lawful means through the court concerned.

74. Defendant of Title Suit No. 38 of 1992 (plaintiff of Title Suit No. 26 of 1992), that is, the present appellant filed Civil Revision No.170 of 2004 before the High Court Division against the judgment and decree passed by the Appellate Court in Title Appeal No.197 of 2002 and the Rule in the civil revision was discharged on the 25th of February, 2007 leading to the filing of the leave, petition (CP No.1568 of 2007). So with the disposal of Title Appeal No.197 of 2002 as affirmed in Civil Revision No.170 of, 2004, by the High Court Division, findings of possession and dispossession given earlier by the Courts below in Title Suit Nos.26 and 38 of 1992 and Title Appeal Nos.57 of 1995 and 182 of 1974 lost all its legal force. In this regard, it is very pertinent to state that the appellant did not file any leave petition against the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2572 of 1998 sending Title Suit No. 38 of 1992 back on remand to the trial Court and thus he allowed Title Suit No.38 of 1992 to be heard and disposed of afresh. And in the instant case, leave has been granted only to decide the point as to whether the learned Judge of the Single Bench correctly interpreted section 56 of the Ordinance as to the power of the Administrator of Waqfs to accord sanction to the mutawalli of the waqf estate to give permanent lease of its immovable property. So, we see no scope of deciding the other points as argued by Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, namely: that before according sanction to the mutawalli to lease out 92 decimals of land of the waqf estate, no enquiry under section 57 of the Ordinance was held and that defendant No. 1 (Moulana Fariduddin Ahmed) failed to prove that he paid the Nazrana and the yearly rent as per terms of the lease deed as well as question of possession and dispossession as alleged by the deceased defendant (predecessor-in-interest of respondent Nos. l(a) and 1(b). In the context, Mr. Mahbubey Alam rightly pointed out that no issue as to the non holding of enquiry by the Administrator of Waqfs under section 57 of the Ordinance was raised in the Courts below and even before the High Court Division. And such a question being fundamentally a question of fact cannot be decided by this Court as a Court of first instance.

75. In order to decide the point on which leave has been granted, we consider it beneficial to quote section 56 of the Ordinance in its entirety. The section reads as under:

56. (1) No transfer by a mutawalli of any immovable property of a waqf by way of sale, gift, mortgage or exchange, or by way of lease for a term exceeding 5 years shall be valid without the previous sanction of the Administrator: Provided that the sanction by the Administrator shall not validate any transfer which is in contravention of any other law for the time being in force or is otherwise invalid.

(2) No Court shall grant permission to any Receiver appointed by the Court for the transfer of any waqf property unless the prior sanction of the Administrator has been obtained.

(3) In the absence of the sanction required by sub-section (1) any transfer made by a mutawalli shall be declared void, if the Administrator, within 4 months of his coming to know of such transfer, or within 3 years from the date of such transfer, whichever is later, applies to the Civil Court in this behalf.

(4) Where a mutawalli transfers a waqf property in contravention of sub-section (1) and afterwards himself becomes the owner of the property, the mutawalli shall, on the direction of the Administrator, reconvey the property to the waqf.

(5) Any transfer made in contravention of the provisions of sub-section (1) shall be deemed to be an act of malfeasance and breach of trust for the purpose of sub-section (1) of section 32".

76. For our purpose sub-sections (2), (3), (4) and of the section are not relevant as admittedly sanction was accorded to the mutawalli by the Administrator of Waqfs to give permanent lease of 92 decimals of land of plot No.932 of the waqf estate.

<u>77. If we carefully see the language of sub-section (1) of section 56 of the Ordinance, it would appear that in case of transfer of any immovable property of a waqf by a mutawalli by way of sale, gift, mortgage or exchange, the only bar has been created by the legislature is that before such transfer previous sanction of the Administrator of Waqfs must be accorded and without such sanction transfer so made shall not be valid. So far as the lease is concerned, the mutawalli has been empowered to lease out any immovable properly of a waqf up to 5 years, and beyond that only with the previous sanction of the Administrator of Waqfs, proviso to the section has given a further rider that even the sanction by the Administrator shall not validate any transfer which is in contravention of any other law for the time being in force or is otherwise invalidate.</u>

78. In the instant case, the deceased mutawalli leased out 1.00 (92+8) acre of land of the waqf in question permanently to the defendant after obtaining previous sanction from the Administrator of Waqfs. It is not the case of the plaintiff-appellant that the sanction by the Administrator in granting lease of the land in question permanently to the defendant was given in contravention of any other law in force at the material time or was otherwise invalid. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan has not also made any submission that the sanction given by the Administrator of Waqf to lease out the land in question was given in contravention of any other law of the land prevalent at the relevant time or was otherwise in valid, so the question of attraction of the proviso to sub-section (1) does not arise at all.

79. Therefore, we are not called upon to make any exercise in that respect. And if we do so that will be mere academic and that will make the judgment unnecessary lengthy.

<u>80. Now, we are to see whether the Administrator of Waqfs acted within his jurisdiction in according the sanction. Another corollary question arises when the legislature has not used the expression permanent lease, but used the expression lease for a term exceeding 5(five) years, that is, in other words has spoken about periodical lease of any immovable property of a waqf can it be said that such sanction also include the power to give sanction to lease out an immovable property of a waqf permanently.</u>

<u>81. The principle of statutory interpretation by which a generic word receives a limited interpretation in the context of a case is well established. In the context, as submitted by Mr Mahmudul Islam, we can legitimately invoke the rule of "noscitur a sociis." This expression means that "the meaning of a word is to be judged by the company it keeps." According to Maxwell the rule "noscitur a sociis" means that, when two or more words which are susceptible of analogous meaning are coupled together they are understood to be used in their cognate sense, they take as it were their colour from each other, that is, the more general is restricted to a sense analogous to a less general.</u>

<u>82. From a mere reading of other words used in sub-section (1) of section 56 of the Ordinance, it is clear that the legislature has created no bar in according sanction by the Administrator of Waqfs to the mutawalli of a waqf estate to transfer its immovable property by way of sale, gift, mortgage or exchange. Transfers by sale, gift, or ex chancre is definitely permanent in nature though as per section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act mortgage is the transfer of an interest in specific "immovable property" for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt, or the performance of an engagement which may give rise to a pecuniary liability. So, when in the same section, the Administrator of Waqfs has been given the power to accord sanction to the mutawalli of a waqf to transfer any of its immovable property by way of sale, gift, or exchange then it will be a too narrow interpretation to say that the legislature did not mean to empower the Administrator of Waqfs to accord sanction to a mutawalli to lease out any immovable property of waqf permanently but only of temporary in nature, that is, periodic lease.</u>

<u>83. In the context, we may also refer to section 33 of the Ordinance. This section has provided that notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in the Ordinance or any other law for the time being in force or in any waqf deed or in any contract, the Administrator may, with the previous sanction of the Government, transfer any part of waqf property for the improvement and benefit of the waqf  (emphasis supplied). So, the legislature has not created any absolute bar from transferring any part of the waqf property, but such transfer must be necessary for the improvement and benefit of the waqf. However, we make it very clear that the power conferred upon the Administrator of Waqfs to accord sanction to a mutawalli of a waqf to transfer any immovable property of a waqf by way of sale, gift, mortgage or exchange or by way of lease for a term exceeding five years or permanent (as in the instant case) by section 56(1) of the Ordinance must be subject to fulfillment of the requirement of section 57 thereof. The section has stipulated 3 (three) obligations to be discharged by the Administrator of Waqfs before according sanction to transfer any immovable property of waqf, these are: (a) to make enquiry by himself for the transfer prayed for (b) to give notice to such persons in such manner as the Administrator thinks fit and (c) hearing them (that is the persons so notified), if they desire to be heard. To us, it appears that the enquiry so made must be in the true sense, that is, it must not be mechanical but transparent as to the necessity for transferring any immovable property of the waqf and the notice must be given to all concerned persons of the waqf particularly, the beneficiaries of the waqf and giving fair chance of hearing to the parties involved in the matter. We do not also see any reason for not reading the conditions or limitations as provided in section 33 of the Ordinance in section 56(1) thereof that before granting sanction the Administrator must be satisfied that such transfer is necessary for the improvement and benefit of the waqf and not to cause any injury, waste or loss of the waqf. In the context, we may recall the pleading of the plaintiff that the lease was granted for the protection of the land of the waqf estate. In the facts and circumstances of the instant case as discussed hereinbefore the principle of law enunciated in the cited cases referred by Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan does not help him. Therefore, we find no substance in the submission of Mr Bhuiyan that since the Administrator of Waqfs has not been vested with the power to accord sanction to the mutawalli of a waqf estate to give permanent lease of any immoveable property of the waqf, the lease deed dated 18-5-1965 executed and registered by the deceased mutawalli on the basis of sanction given by the Administrator of Waqfs was void and by such deed defendant No. 1 acquired no right, title and interest in the lease hold land, that is, the suit land.</u>

84. From the judgment passed in Title Appeal No.197 of 2002, it appears that the Appellate Court being the last Court of fact considered the evidence on record regarding the possession and the dispossession of the con-tending parties including the appellant and came to the specific finding that after the lease deed dated 18-5-1965, the plaintiff got possession of the leasehold land and then he was dispossessed from 3 decimals of land as described in the second schedule to the plaint (of Title Suit No.38 of 1992) . From the impugned judgment and order (passed in Civil Revision No.170 of 2004), it appears that none appeared in support of the Rule when the same was taken up for hearing. The learned Judge of the single Bench made the Rule absolute affirming those of the Appellate Court on the finding as follows:

"I have considered the ground taken in the revisional application which are general in nature and do no find any ground for misreading of evidence or non consideration of evidence or misconstruction of evidence and thus I do not find any merit in this rule."

85. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan could not point out any perversity in the finding of possession and dispossession arrived at by the Appellate Court, consequently we find no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and order passed in Civil Revision No. 170 of 2004.

86. For the discussions made above, we do not find any merit in the appeal and in the leave petition.

87. Accordingly, the appeal and the leave petition are dismissed. But we make no order as to costs.
